Huntingdon
HUNT-ing-dun
n. (the Ouse town and county of Huntingdonshire, with an Augustinian priory, and the title borne by Selina Hastings, patroness of the evangelical revival)
Old English Huntandun, the huntsman's hill, from hunta, a hunter, and dun, a hill.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Huntingdon is a small town on the Great Ouse, the county town of the old county of Huntingdonshire, with an Augustinian priory founded in the twelfth century and dissolved in 1538. Oliver Cromwell was born there in 1599 and represented it in parliament. The name belongs to church history chiefly through the earldom: Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, widowed in 1746, spent nearly the whole of a great fortune on the evangelical revival, built or bought some sixty chapels, appointed Whitefield and other preachers as her chaplains, founded Trevecca College in Wales for training preachers, and in the end was forced by the Toleration Act proceedings of 1779 to register her chapels as dissenting, which created the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion. The dictionary records Huntingdon for what she did with money. Scripture is specific about the uses of property in the hands of believers: goods are sold and parted as men have need, bread is dealt to the hungry, and the religion God calls pure is defined by the visiting of the fatherless and widows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a possession as that which is owned; to part as to divide and distribute; need as want and necessity; to deal as to distribute; and pure as free from defilement.

expand to see more

POSSESSION, n. The having, holding or detention of property in one's power or command; the thing possessed.

PART, v.t. To divide; to separate; to sever; to distribute among; to share.

NEED, n. Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state that requires supply or relief; poverty.

DEAL, v.t. To divide; to part; to separate; to distribute; to give in portions.

PURE, a. Separate from all heterogeneous matter; free from moral defilement; genuine; real; unmixed.

Key Scripture

Act 2:45 — "And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need."

Isa 58:7 — "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?"

Mat 25:35 — "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:"

Jam 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Modern Corruption

Ouse town of the old county of Huntingdonshire, whose countess Selina Hastings spent a fortune on chapels, chaplains and Trevecca College for the revival.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that property in a believer's hands is for distribution. Luke reports the Jerusalem church doing it plainly: “And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need” (Act 2:45). Isaiah had already specified what the fast God chooses actually consists of, “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7).

The live temptation for a wealthy patron is to treat the gospel as a cause to be sponsored rather than a word to be obeyed, and the Countess avoided it by the simple method of being present: she sat under the preaching she paid for and answered to the law when her chapels were challenged. Christ counts the plain acts as done to himself, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and James fixes the definition that a chapel-building programme cannot replace: pure religion is “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ktema (G2933), a possession; Greek diamerizo (G1266), to distribute; Hebrew paras (H6536), to break or divide bread; Greek threskeia (G2356), religious observance.

expand to see more

Greek ktema (G2933) — a possession, an estate; “sold their possessions and goods”, Acts 2:45.

Greek diamerizo (G1266) — to divide up, to distribute; “parted them to all men, as every man had need”, Acts 2:45.

Hebrew paras (H6536) — to break in pieces, to divide; “to deal thy bread to the hungry”, Isaiah 58:7.

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a guest; “I was a stranger, and ye took me in”, Matthew 25:35.

Greek threskeia (G2356) — religious service; “Pure religion and undefiled”, James 1:27.

Usage

"“parted them to all men, as every man had need” (Act 2:45) — what a fortune is for."

"“Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) — the fast God chooses."

"“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) — what no building replaces."
